title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Prince Andrew had spent two years continuously in the country.

All the plans Pierre had attempted on his estates — constantly switching from one thing to another without finishing any of them — were carried out by Prince Andrew quietly and without apparent effort.
He possessed to the highest degree a practical tenacity that Pierre lacked, and without fuss or strain this quality set things in motion.

On one of his estates, three hundred serfs were liberated and became free agricultural laborers — one of the first such examples in Russia. On other estates, the serfs' compulsory labor was replaced by a cash payment. A trained midwife was hired for Bogucharovo at his expense, and a priest was paid to teach the peasants' and household serfs' children reading and writing.

Prince Andrew spent half his time at Bald Hills with his father and his son, who was still in the care of nurses. The other half he spent in "Bogucharovo Cloister," as his father called Prince Andrew's estate. Despite the indifference to the world's affairs he had professed to Pierre, he diligently followed everything that was happening. He received many books and was surprised to find that when visitors came from Petersburg — the very center of life — they were actually behind him, despite his never leaving the country, in their knowledge of both domestic and foreign affairs.

Besides managing his estates and reading widely, Prince Andrew was at this time working on a critical analysis of the two most recent, unsuccessful campaigns and drafting a proposal for reforming the army's rules and regulations.
In the spring of 1809 he went to visit the Ryazan estates that his son had inherited and of which he was guardian.

Warmed by the spring sunshine, he sat in the open carriage looking at the new grass, the first leaves on the birch trees, and the first puffs of white cloud floating across the clear blue sky. He wasn't thinking about anything in particular, but gazed around cheerfully and absent-mindedly.

They crossed the ferry where he had talked with Pierre the year before. They went through the muddy village, past threshing floors and green fields of winter rye, downhill where snow still lingered near the bridge, uphill where the clay had been liquefied by rain, past strips of stubble and bushes touched with green here and there, and into a birch forest that lined both sides of the road. In the forest it was almost hot — no wind could be felt. The birches with their sticky green leaves stood motionless, and lilac flowers and the first blades of green grass pushed up through last year's fallen leaves. The dark evergreen of the small fir trees scattered among the birches was an unwelcome reminder of winter. Entering the forest, the horses began to snort and broke into a visible sweat.
Peter, the footman, said something to the coachman; the latter agreed. But apparently the coachman's agreement wasn't enough for Peter, who turned on the box toward his master.
"How pleasant it is, your excellency!" he said with a respectful smile.
"What?"
"It's pleasant, your excellency!"

"What is he talking about?" thought Prince Andrew. "Oh — the spring, I suppose," he thought, glancing around. "Yes, everything is green already. How early! The birches, the cherry trees, and the alders too are coming out. But the oaks show no sign yet. Ah — there's one!"

At the edge of the road stood an oak. Probably ten times the age of the birch trees that formed the forest, it was ten times as thick and twice as tall. It was an enormous tree, its girth twice what a man could embrace, and clearly long ago some of its branches had been broken off and its bark scarred. With its huge, ungainly limbs sprawling asymmetrically, its gnarled hands and fingers, it stood like an aged, stern, scornful giant among the smiling birch trees. Only the dead-looking evergreen firs scattered through the forest and this oak refused to yield to the charm of spring or acknowledge either the sunshine or the season.

"Spring, love, happiness!" this oak seemed to say. "Aren't you tired of that stupid, meaningless, endlessly repeated fraud? Always the same, and always a sham. There is no spring, no sun, no happiness! Look at those stunted dead firs — always the same. And look at me, sticking out my broken and scarred limbs wherever they've grown — from my back, from my sides. As they grew, so I stand — and I don't believe in your hopes and your lies."

As he drove through the forest, Prince Andrew turned several times to look at that oak, as if expecting something from it. Under the oak too there were flowers and grass, but it stood among them scowling, rigid, misshapen, and grim as ever.
"Yes, the oak is right — a thousand times right," thought Prince Andrew. "Let others — the young — fall for that fraud again, but we know life. Our life is finished!"

A whole sequence of new thoughts — hopeless but strangely pleasant in their melancholy — rose in his mind in connection with that tree. During this journey he reconsidered his life, as it were, from scratch, and arrived at his old conclusion — comforting in its hopelessness: that there was nothing for him to begin, that he must simply live out his days, content to do no harm, and not troubling himself or wishing for anything.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: Pierre didn't stay for dinner but left the room and went away at once. He drove through the town looking for Anatole Kuragin, at the thought of whom the blood rushed to his heart and he felt difficulty breathing. He was not at the ice hills, nor at the gypsies', nor at Komoneno's. Pierre drove to the Club. At the Club all was going on as usual. The members gathering for dinner were sitting in groups; they greeted Pierre and spoke of the town news. The footman, knowing his habits and acquaintances, told him there was a place left for him in the small dining room, and that Prince Michael Zakharych was in the library, but that Paul Timofeevich had not yet arrived. One of Pierre's acquaintances, while chatting about the weather, asked if he had heard about Kuragin's abduction of Rostova — which was the talk of the town — and was it true? Pierre laughed and said it was nonsense, as he had just come from the Rostovs'. He asked everyone about Anatole. One man told him he hadn't come yet, and another that he was expected for dinner. Pierre felt it strange to see this calm, indifferent crowd of people who were unaware of what was going on in his soul. He paced through the ballroom, waited till everyone had arrived, and as Anatole didn't show up, didn't stay for dinner but drove home.

Anatole, whom Pierre was looking for, dined that day with Dolokhov, consulting him about how to fix this unfortunate business. It seemed essential to him to see Natasha. In the evening he drove to his sister's to discuss with her how to arrange a meeting. When Pierre returned home after vainly hunting all over Moscow, his valet informed him that Prince Anatole was with the countess. The countess's drawing room was full of guests.
Pierre, without greeting his wife — whom he had not seen since his return, and at that moment found more repulsive than ever — entered the drawing room and seeing Anatole went up to him.
"Ah, Pierre," said the countess, going up to her husband. "You don't know what trouble our Anatole..."

She stopped, seeing in the forward thrust of her husband's head, in his glowing eyes and his determined stride, the terrible signs of that rage and power she knew and had herself experienced after his duel with Dolokhov.
"Where you are, there is vice and evil!" said Pierre to his wife. "Anatole, come with me! I must speak to you," he added in French.
Anatole glanced at his sister and rose obediently, ready to follow Pierre. Pierre, taking him by the arm, pulled him toward himself and led him from the room.
"If you make a scene in my drawing room..." Helene whispered, but Pierre didn't reply and went out.
Anatole followed him with his usual casual step, but his face showed anxiety.
Having entered his study, Pierre closed the door and addressed Anatole without looking at him.
"You promised Countess Rostova to marry her and were about to elope with her — is that so?"
"My dear fellow," answered Anatole (their whole conversation was in French), "I don't consider myself obliged to answer questions put to me in that tone."

Pierre's face, already pale, became distorted with fury. He seized Anatole by the collar of his uniform with his big hand and shook him from side to side until Anatole's face showed sufficient terror.
"When I tell you that I must talk to you!..." repeated Pierre.
"Come now, this is ridiculous. What?" said Anatole, fingering a button on his collar that had been torn loose with a bit of cloth.
"You're a scoundrel and a villain, and I don't know what stops me from the pleasure of smashing your skull with this!" said Pierre — expressing himself so stiffly because he was speaking French.
He took a heavy paperweight and lifted it threateningly, but at once put it back in its place.
"Did you promise to marry her?"
"I... I didn't think of it. I never promised, because..."
Pierre interrupted him.
"Have you any letters of hers? Any letters?" he said, moving toward Anatole.
Anatole glanced at him and immediately thrust his hand into his pocket and drew out his wallet.
Pierre took the letter Anatole handed him and, pushing aside a table that stood in his way, threw himself on the sofa.

"I won't be violent, don't be afraid!" said Pierre in answer to a frightened gesture of Anatole's. "First — the letters," said he, as if reciting a lesson to himself. "Second," he continued after a short pause, rising again and pacing the room, "tomorrow you must get out of Moscow."
"But how can I?..."

"Third," Pierre went on without listening, "you must never breathe a word of what has passed between you and Countess Rostova. I know I can't prevent your doing so, but if you have a spark of conscience..." Pierre paced the room several times in silence.
Anatole sat at a table, frowning and biting his lips.

"After all, you must understand that besides your pleasure there is such a thing as other people's happiness and peace, and that you are ruining a whole life for the sake of your own amusement! Amuse yourself with women like my wife — with them you're within your rights, for they know what you want of them. They are armed against you by the same experience of depravity. But to promise a young girl to marry her... to deceive, to kidnap... Don't you understand that it is as contemptible as beating an old man or a child?..."
Pierre paused and looked at Anatole no longer with anger but with a questioning look.

"I don't know about that, eh?" said Anatole, growing more confident as Pierre mastered his fury. "I don't know that and don't want to," he said, not looking at Pierre and with a slight tremor of his lower jaw, "but you've used such words to me — 'contemptible' and so on — which as a man of honor I can't allow anyone to use."
Pierre looked at him with amazement, unable to understand what he wanted.
"Though it was a private conversation," Anatole continued, "still I can't..."
"Are you looking for satisfaction?" said Pierre ironically.
"You could at least take back your words. What? If you want me to do as you wish, eh?"
"I take them back, I take them back!" said Pierre, "and I ask you to forgive me." Pierre involuntarily glanced at the torn button. "And if you need money for your journey..."
Anatole smiled. The expression of that base and cringing smile, which Pierre knew so well in his wife, revolted him.
"Oh, vile and heartless breed!" he exclaimed, and left the room.
The next day Anatole left for Petersburg.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: On the morning of the twenty-fifth, Pierre was leaving Mozhaysk. At the descent of the high, steep hill where a winding road led out of town past the cathedral on the right—where a service was being held and the bells were ringing—Pierre got out of his carriage and continued on foot. Behind him a cavalry regiment was coming down the hill, preceded by its singers. Coming up toward him was a train of carts carrying men wounded in the previous day's engagement. The peasant drivers, shouting and lashing their horses, kept crossing from side to side. The carts, each holding three or four wounded soldiers lying or sitting, jolted over the stones thrown on the steep slope to form something like a road. The wounded, bandaged with rags, with pale cheeks, compressed lips, and knitted brows, gripped the sides of the carts as they jolted against one another. Almost all of them stared with naive, childlike curiosity at Pierre's white hat and green tailcoat.

Pierre's coachman shouted angrily at the convoy of wounded to keep to one side of the road. The cavalry regiment, descending the hill with its singers, surrounded Pierre's carriage and blocked the road. Pierre stopped, pressed against the side of the road cut into the hillside. The sunshine from behind the hill didn't reach into the cut, and there it was cold and damp, but above Pierre's head was the bright August sun and the bells rang merrily. One of the carts of wounded stopped by the roadside close to Pierre. The driver in his bast shoes ran panting up to it, placed a stone under one of the rear wheels, and began adjusting the harness on his small horse.
One of the wounded, an old soldier with a bandaged arm who was walking alongside the cart, caught hold of it with his good hand and turned to look at Pierre.
"I say, countryman! Will they set us down here or take us on to Moscow?" he asked.

Pierre was so deep in thought that he didn't hear the question. He was looking now at the cavalry regiment that had met the convoy of wounded, now at the cart beside him, in which two wounded men were sitting and one was lying. One of those sitting up had probably been hit in the cheek. His whole head was wrapped in bandages and one cheek was swollen to the size of a baby's head. His nose and mouth were twisted to one side. This soldier was looking at the cathedral and crossing himself. Another, a young recruit as pale as if there were no blood in his thin face, looked at Pierre kindly with a fixed smile. The third lay face down so that his face was hidden. The cavalry singers were passing close by:
Ah lost, quite lost... is my head so keen, Living in a foreign land...
they sang their soldiers' marching song.

As if in response to them, but with a different kind of merriment, the metallic sound of the bells rang out high above, and the hot rays of the sun bathed the top of the opposite slope with yet another sort of joy. But below the slope, by the cart with the wounded and the panting little horse where Pierre stood, it was damp, somber, and sad.
The soldier with the swollen cheek looked angrily at the cavalry singers.
"Oh, the show-offs!" he muttered reproachfully.

"It's not just the soldiers—I've seen peasants today too... The peasants—even they have to go," said the soldier behind the cart, addressing Pierre with a sad smile. "No distinctions nowadays... They want the whole nation to attack them—in a word, it's Moscow! They want to make an end of it."
Despite the vagueness of the soldier's words, Pierre understood what he meant and nodded in agreement.
The road cleared again; Pierre descended the hill and drove on.

He kept looking to either side of the road for familiar faces but saw only the unfamiliar faces of soldiers from various branches of the service, all of whom stared with astonishment at his white hat and green tailcoat.

Having gone nearly three miles, he at last met an acquaintance and eagerly called out to him. This was one of the senior army doctors. He was driving toward Pierre in a covered gig, sitting beside a young surgeon, and on recognizing Pierre told the Cossack in the driver's seat to stop.
"Count! Your excellency, what brings you here?" asked the doctor.
"Well, you know, I wanted to see..."
"Yes, yes, there will be something to see..."
Pierre got out and talked to the doctor, explaining his intention of being present at the battle.
The doctor advised him to apply directly to Kutuzov.

"Why should you be God knows where, out of sight, during the battle?" he said, exchanging glances with his young companion. "In any case, his Serene Highness knows you and will receive you graciously. That's what you must do."
The doctor seemed tired and in a hurry.
"You think so?... I also wanted to ask—where exactly is our position?" said Pierre.
"The position?" the doctor repeated. "Well, that's not my area. Drive past Tatarinova; there's a lot of digging going on there. Go up the hill and you'll see."
"You can see from there?... If you would..."
But the doctor interrupted him and moved toward his gig.

"I'd go with you, but honestly I'm up to here"—he pointed to his throat. "I'm racing to the corps commander. How do things stand?... You know, Count, there'll be a battle tomorrow. Out of a hundred thousand, we must expect at least twenty thousand wounded, and we haven't enough stretchers, beds, medics, or doctors for six thousand. We have ten thousand carts, but we need other things too—we'll just have to manage."

The strange thought that of the thousands of men—young and old—who had stared with cheerful surprise at his hat (perhaps the very men he had noticed), twenty thousand were doomed to wounds and death, struck Pierre forcefully.

"They may die tomorrow; why are they thinking about anything but death?" And by some hidden chain of thought, the descent of the Mozhaysk hill, the carts with the wounded, the ringing bells, the slanting rays of the sun, and the cavalrymen's songs vividly recurred to him.

"The cavalry ride to battle and meet the wounded and don't give a moment's thought to what awaits them, but ride past winking at the wounded. Yet from among these men, twenty thousand are doomed to die—and they wonder at my hat! Strange!" thought Pierre, continuing toward Tatarinova.

In front of a landowner's house to the left of the road stood carriages, wagons, and crowds of orderlies and sentries. The commander in chief was staying there, but when Pierre arrived he was not in, and hardly any of the staff were present—they had gone to the church service. Pierre drove on toward Gorki.

When he had climbed the hill and reached the little village street, he saw for the first time peasant militiamen in their white shirts and with crosses on their caps, who, talking and laughing loudly, lively and sweating, were at work on a huge knoll overgrown with grass to the right of the road.
Some of them were digging, others wheeling barrowloads of earth along planks, while others stood around doing nothing.

Two officers stood on the knoll directing the men. Seeing these peasants, who were clearly still amused by the novelty of their position as soldiers, Pierre once again thought of the wounded at Mozhaysk and understood what the soldier had meant when he said: "They want the whole nation to attack them." The sight of these bearded peasants working on the battlefield, with their clumsy boots, sweating necks, and shirts open from the left to the middle, exposing their sunburned collarbones, impressed Pierre more powerfully with the solemnity and importance of the moment than anything he had yet seen or heard.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: Pierre got out of his carriage and, passing the toiling militiamen, climbed the knoll from which, according to the doctor, the battlefield could be seen.
It was about eleven o'clock. The sun was somewhat to the left and behind him, and brightly illuminated the enormous panorama that rose like an amphitheater before him in the clear, thin air.

From the upper left, cutting through that amphitheater, wound the Smolensk highway, passing through a village with a white church about five hundred paces ahead of the knoll and below it. This was Borodino. Below the village the road crossed the river by a bridge and, winding down and up, rose higher and higher to the village of Valuevo, visible about four miles away, where Napoleon was then stationed. Beyond Valuevo the road vanished into a yellowing forest on the horizon. Far in the distance in that birch and fir forest to the right of the road, the cross and belfry of the Kolocha Monastery gleamed in the sun. Scattered over the whole blue expanse, to right and left of the forest and the road, smoking campfires could be seen and indistinct masses of troops—ours and the enemy's. The ground to the right—along the course of the Kolocha and Moskva rivers—was broken and hilly. Between the hollows, the villages of Bezubova and Zakharino were visible in the distance. On the left the ground was more level; there were grain fields, and the smoking ruins of Semenovsk, which had been burned, could be seen.

Everything Pierre saw was so indistinct that neither the left nor the right side of the field matched what he had expected. Nowhere could he see the battlefield he had imagined—only fields, meadows, troops, woods, campfire smoke, villages, hills, and streams; and try as he might, he could make out no military "position" in this place teeming with life, nor could he even tell our troops from the enemy's.
"I need to ask someone who knows," he thought, and approached an officer who was looking with curiosity at his huge, unmilitary figure.
"May I ask," said Pierre, "what village that is ahead?"
"Burdino, isn't it?" said the officer, turning to his companion.
"Borodino," the other corrected him.
The officer, clearly glad of a chance to talk, moved up to Pierre.
"Are those our men there?" Pierre asked.
"Yes, and farther on are the French," said the officer. "There they are, there... you can see them."
"Where? Where?" asked Pierre.
"You can see them with the naked eye... Look, there!"
The officer pointed toward the smoke visible to the left beyond the river, and the same stern and serious expression Pierre had noticed on many faces that day came over his own.
"Ah, those are the French! And over there?" Pierre pointed to a knoll on the left, near which some troops were visible.
"Those are ours."
"And there?" Pierre pointed to another knoll in the distance with a big tree on it, near a village in a hollow where campfires were smoking and something dark could be seen.
"That's his again," said the officer. (It was the Shevardino Redoubt.) "It was ours yesterday, but now it's his."
"Then where's our position?"

"Our position?" replied the officer with a satisfied smile. "I can tell you quite clearly, because I built nearly all our fortifications. There, you see? There's our center, at Borodino, right there," and he pointed to the village with the white church ahead. "That's where you cross the Kolocha. You see down there where the rows of hay are in the hollow? That's the bridge. That's our center. Our right flank is over there"—he pointed sharply to the right, far away in the broken ground—"that's where the Moskva River is, and we've built three very strong redoubts there. The left flank..." Here the officer paused. "Well, you see, that's harder to explain... Yesterday our left flank was there at Shevardino, you see, where the oak is, but now we've pulled our left wing back—now it's over there, do you see that village and the smoke? That's Semenovsk, yes, there," he pointed to Raevsky's knoll. "But the battle probably won't be there. His having moved his troops there is just a feint; he'll probably swing around to the right of the Moskva. But wherever it may be, many a man won't be here tomorrow!" he added.
An elderly sergeant who had come up while the officer was speaking had waited silently for him to finish, but at this point, evidently not liking the officer's remark, interrupted him.
"Gabions need to be sent for," he said sternly.
The officer looked embarrassed, as though he understood one might think about how many men would be missing tomorrow but shouldn't say it aloud.
"Well, send third company again," the officer said quickly.
"And you—are you one of the doctors?"
"No, I've come on my own," answered Pierre, and he went back down the hill, passing the militiamen.
"Oh, those damned fellows!" muttered the officer, following him and holding his nose as he ran past the working men.
"There they are... bringing her, coming... There they are... They'll be here in a minute..." voices were suddenly heard, and officers, soldiers, and militiamen began running forward along the road.
A church procession was coming up the hill from Borodino. First along the dusty road came infantry in ranks, bareheaded and with arms reversed. From behind them came the sound of church singing.
Soldiers and militiamen ran bareheaded past Pierre toward the procession.
"They're bringing her—our Protectress!... The Iberian Mother of God!" someone cried.
"The Smolensk Mother of God," another corrected him.

The militiamen—both those who had been in the village and those who had been working on the battery—threw down their shovels and ran to meet the church procession. Following the battalion that marched along the dusty road came priests in their vestments—one little old man in a hood with attendants and singers. Behind them, soldiers and officers carried a large, dark-faced icon in an embossed metal cover. This was the icon that had been brought from Smolensk and had since accompanied the army. Behind, before, and on both sides, crowds of militiamen with bared heads walked, ran, and bowed to the ground.

At the top of the hill they stopped with the icon; the men who had been holding it up by the linen bands were relieved by others, the chanters relit their censers, and the service began. The hot rays of the sun beat straight down, and a fresh soft wind played with the hair of the bared heads and with the ribbons decorating the icon. The singing didn't sound loud under the open sky. An immense crowd of bareheaded officers, soldiers, and militiamen surrounded the icon. Behind the priest and chanter stood the dignitaries in a reserved spot. A bald general with a Saint George's Cross on his neck stood just behind the priest, and without crossing himself (he was evidently a German) patiently waited for the service to end, which he considered it necessary to attend, probably to arouse the Russian people's patriotism. Another general stood in a martial pose, crossing himself with a quick motion of his hand before his chest while looking about him. Standing among the crowd of peasants, Pierre recognized several acquaintances among these notables but didn't look at them—his whole attention was absorbed by the serious expression on the faces of the soldiers and militiamen, who were all gazing intently at the icon. As soon as the tired chanters, who were singing the service for the twentieth time that day, began lazily and mechanically to sing, "Save from calamity Your servants, O Mother of God," and the priest and deacon chimed in, "For to You under God we all flee as to an unbreakable wall and protection," there again kindled in all those faces the same expression of awareness of the solemnity of the approaching moment that Pierre had seen at the foot of the hill at Mozhaysk and fleetingly on the many faces he had met that morning; and heads bowed more often, hair was tossed back, and sighs and the sound of men crossing themselves were heard.
The crowd around the icon suddenly parted and pressed against Pierre. Someone—a very important person, judging by the haste with which way was made—was approaching the icon.
It was Kutuzov, who had been riding around the position and on his way back to Tatarinova had stopped where the service was being held. Pierre recognized him at once by his distinctive figure.

With a long overcoat on his extremely stout, round-shouldered body, with his uncovered white head and puffy face showing the white ball of the eye he had lost, Kutuzov walked with a plunging, swaying gait into the crowd and stopped behind the priest. He crossed himself with a practiced movement, reached down and touched the ground with his hand, and bowed his white head with a deep sigh. Behind Kutuzov was Bennigsen and the suite. Despite the commander in chief's presence, which attracted the attention of all the senior officers, the militiamen and soldiers continued their prayers without looking at him.

When the service was over, Kutuzov stepped up to the icon, sank heavily to his knees, bowed to the ground, and for a long time tried in vain to rise but could not because of his weakness and weight. His white head twitched with the effort. At last he rose, kissed the icon as a child does with naively pouting lips, and again bowed until he touched the ground with his hand. The other generals followed his example, then the officers, and after them, with excited faces, pressing on one another, crowding, panting, and pushing, came the soldiers and militiamen.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 32
paragraphs: Beside himself with terror, Pierre jumped up and ran back to the battery as the only refuge from the horrors surrounding him.

Entering the earthwork, he noticed men doing something there but no shots being fired from the battery. He didn't have time to register who these men were. He saw the senior officer lying on the earth wall with his back turned, as if examining something below, and that one of the soldiers he'd noticed before was struggling forward shouting "Brothers!" while trying to free himself from men holding his arm. He saw something else strange too.

But he didn't have time to realize that the colonel had been killed, that the soldier shouting "Brothers!" was a prisoner, or that another man had been bayoneted in the back before his eyes — because hardly had he run into the redoubt when a thin, sallow-faced, sweating man in a blue uniform rushed at him sword in hand, shouting something. Instinctively bracing against the impact — for they had been running at full speed toward each other before either saw the other — Pierre put out his hands and seized the man (a French officer) by the shoulder with one hand and by the throat with the other. The officer dropped his sword and grabbed Pierre by the collar.

For several seconds they stared with frightened eyes at each other's unfamiliar faces, both bewildered by what they had done and what to do next. "Am I the prisoner, or have I taken him prisoner?" each was thinking. But the French officer was more inclined to think he'd been captured, because Pierre's strong hand, driven by instinctive fear, squeezed his throat ever tighter. The Frenchman was about to say something when, just above their heads, a cannonball whistled by — terribly low — and it seemed to Pierre that the French officer's head had been torn off, so fast had he ducked.

Pierre ducked his head too and let his hands fall. Without further thought about who had captured whom, the Frenchman ran back to the battery and Pierre ran down the slope, stumbling over the dead and wounded who seemed to clutch at his feet. But before he reached the bottom of the knoll, he was met by a dense crowd of Russian soldiers who, stumbling, tripping, and shouting, ran merrily and wildly toward the battery. (This was the attack for which Ermolov claimed credit, declaring that only his courage and luck made such a feat possible — the attack during which he supposedly tossed St. George's Crosses from his pocket into the battery for the first soldiers who reached it.)
The French who had occupied the battery fled, and our troops, shouting "Hurrah!" chased them so far beyond the battery that it was hard to call them back.

The prisoners were brought down from the battery, including a wounded French general whom the officers surrounded. Crowds of wounded — some Pierre knew, some he didn't — Russians and French alike, with faces twisted in pain, walked, crawled, and were carried on stretchers from the battery. Pierre went back up onto the knoll where he had spent over an hour, and of that family circle that had welcomed him as a member, not a single one remained. There were many dead he didn't recognize, but some he knew. The young officer still sat the same way, doubled over, in a pool of blood at the edge of the earth wall. The red-faced man was still twitching, but they didn't carry him away.
Pierre ran down the slope once more.
"Now they will stop it — now they will be horrified at what they have done!" he thought, walking aimlessly toward a crowd of stretcher-bearers moving from the battlefield.

But behind the veil of smoke the sun was still high, and in front — especially to the left near Semenovsk — something seemed to be seething in the haze, and the roar of cannon and musketry did not weaken but grew even more desperate, like a man straining to scream with all his remaining strength.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Moscow's last day had come. It was a clear, bright autumn day — a Sunday. The church bells rang for service everywhere, just as usual on Sundays. Nobody yet seemed to realize what awaited the city.

Only two things hinted at Moscow's social condition — the rabble (the poor people) and the price of goods. An enormous crowd of factory workers, house servants, and peasants, mixed with some officials, seminarians, and gentry, had gone early that morning to the Three Hills. Having waited there for Rostopchin, who didn't show up, they became convinced Moscow would be surrendered and then scattered through the city to taverns and cookshops. Prices also told the story. Weapons, gold, carts, and horses kept rising in price, while the value of paper money and city goods kept falling. By midday there were cases of carters hauling valuable cloth and receiving only half its value as payment, while peasant horses fetched five hundred rubles each and furniture, mirrors, and bronzes were being given away for nothing.

In the Rostovs' staid, old-fashioned household, the dissolution of former conditions was barely noticeable. As for the servants, the only sign was that three of their huge retinue disappeared during the night, but nothing was stolen. As for the value of their possessions, the thirty peasant carts from their estates — which many people envied — proved extremely valuable, with enormous sums offered for them. Not only were huge amounts offered for the horses and carts, but the previous evening and early on the morning of September 1, orderlies and servants sent by wounded officers came to the Rostovs', and wounded men dragged themselves there from neighboring houses, begging the servants to try to get them a ride out of Moscow. The major-domo, to whom these pleas were addressed, felt sorry for the wounded but firmly refused, saying he didn't dare even mention it to the count. However much one pitied these wounded men, it was clear that giving one cart meant there'd be no reason to refuse another, or all the carts, or the family's own carriages. Thirty carts couldn't save all the wounded, and in a general catastrophe one couldn't ignore one's own family. So the major-domo reasoned on his master's behalf.

Waking up that morning, Count Ilya Rostov slipped quietly from the bedroom so as not to wake the countess, who had fallen asleep only near dawn, and came out to the porch in his lilac silk dressing gown. In the yard the loaded carts stood roped and ready. The carriages were at the front porch. The major-domo stood at the porch talking to an elderly orderly and a pale young officer with a bandaged arm. Seeing the count, the major-domo made a significant, stern gesture for both of them to leave.
"Well, Vasilich, is everything ready?" asked the count, and stroking his bald head he looked good-naturedly at the officer and orderly, nodding to them. (He liked seeing new faces.)
"We can harness up at once, your excellency."
"Good. As soon as the countess wakes, we'll be off, God willing! What is it, gentlemen?" he added, turning to the officer. "Are you staying in my house?"
The officer stepped closer, and suddenly his face flushed crimson.
"Count, please — for God's sake — allow me to squeeze into a corner of one of your carts! I have nothing with me here. I'll be fine on a loaded cart..."
Before the officer had finished, the orderly made the same request on behalf of his master.

"Oh, yes, yes, yes!" the count said hastily. "I'll be very happy to. Vasilich, you'll see to it. Just unload a cart or two. Well, what of it — do what's needed," he said, muttering some vague instruction.

But at the same moment, an expression of warm gratitude on the officer's face had already sealed the order. The count looked around. In the yard, at the gates, at the windows of the wings, wounded officers and their orderlies could be seen. They were all looking at the count and moving toward the porch.
"Please step into the gallery, your excellency," said the major-domo. "What are your instructions about the pictures?"
The count went inside with him, repeating his order not to refuse any wounded man asking for a ride.
"Well, some of the things can be unloaded," he added softly and confidentially, as though afraid of being overheard.

At nine o'clock the countess woke, and Matrena Timofeevna — who had been her lady's maid before her marriage and now served as a sort of chief enforcer — came to report that Madame Schoss was very upset and the young ladies' summer dresses couldn't be left behind. On inquiry, the countess learned that Madame Schoss was offended because her trunk had been removed from its cart — all the loads were being untied and the luggage taken out to make room for wounded men, whom the count, in the simplicity of his heart, had ordered to be taken along. The countess sent for her husband.
"What is this, my dear? I hear the luggage is being unloaded."

"You know, love, I wanted to tell you... dear Countess... an officer came asking for a few carts for the wounded. After all, our things can be replaced — but think what being left behind means to them! Really, in our own yard — we invited them in ourselves, and there are officers among them. You know, I think, my dear... let them have the carts... where's the hurry?"

The count spoke timidly, as he always did when discussing money. The countess was used to this tone as a warning of something bad for the children's interests — like building a new gallery or conservatory, or starting a private theater or orchestra. She was accustomed always to resist anything announced in that timid tone, and considered it her duty.

She put on her dolefully submissive manner and said to her husband: "Listen, Count — you've managed things so that we're getting nothing for the house, and now you want to throw away all our — all the children's property! You said yourself we have a hundred thousand rubles' worth of things in this house. I don't agree, my dear, I don't! Do as you like! It's the government's job to look after the wounded — they know how. Look at the Lopukhins across the street — they cleared everything out two days ago. That's what other people do. Only we are such fools. If you have no pity on me, at least think of the children."
Waving his arms in despair, the count left the room without answering.
"Papa! What are you doing?" asked Natasha, who had followed him into her mother's room.
"Nothing! What business is it of yours?" the count muttered angrily.
"But I heard," said Natasha. "Why does Mama object?"
"What business is it of yours?" the count snapped.
Natasha walked to the window and stood thinking.
"Papa! Here comes Berg to see us," she said, looking out.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Berg, the Rostovs' son-in-law, was already a colonel wearing the orders of Vladimir and Anna, and still held his quiet, agreeable post as assistant to the head of staff of the assistant commander of the First Division of the Second Army.
On September 1 he had come to Moscow from the army.

He had no real business in Moscow, but he'd noticed that everyone in the army was requesting leave to go there, each with something to attend to. So he felt it necessary to request leave too, for family and domestic reasons.

Berg drove up to his father-in-law's house in his neat little trap drawn by a pair of sleek roans — exactly like those of a certain prince. He looked carefully at the carts in the yard and, while walking up to the porch, pulled out a clean handkerchief and tied a knot in it.
From the anteroom Berg hurried with smooth but eager steps into the drawing room, embraced the count, kissed the hands of Natasha and Sonya, and rushed to ask about "Mama's" health.
"Health — at a time like this?" said the count. "Come, tell us the news! Is the army retreating, or will there be another battle?"

"Only God Almighty can decide the fate of our fatherland, Papa," said Berg. "The army is burning with heroic spirit and the leaders have, so to speak, now assembled in council. No one knows what's coming. But in general I can tell you, Papa, that such a heroic spirit, the truly ancient valor of the Russian army, which they — which it" — he corrected himself — "displayed in the battle of the twenty-sixth — there are no words worthy of it! I tell you, Papa" — he smote his breast as a general he'd heard speaking had done, though Berg did it slightly late, since the gesture should have accompanied the words "Russian army" — "I tell you frankly that we officers, far from having to urge the men on, could hardly restrain those... those heroic feats of ancient valor," he went on rapidly. "General Barclay de Tolly risked his life everywhere at the head of the troops, I assure you. Our corps was positioned on a hillside. You can imagine!"

And Berg recounted everything he remembered from the various stories he'd heard in recent days. Natasha watched him with an intent gaze that seemed to confuse him, as if she were trying to find in his face the answer to some question.

"The heroism displayed by the Russian warriors is altogether beyond imagination or adequate praise!" said Berg, glancing at Natasha, and as if trying to win her over, replying to her steady look with a smile. "'Russia is not in Moscow — she lives in the hearts of her sons!' Isn't that right, Papa?" he said.

Just then the countess came in from the sitting room with a weary, discontented expression. Berg jumped up, kissed her hand, asked about her health, and, tilting his head from side to side to express sympathy, stood beside her.
"Yes, Mama, I tell you honestly, these are difficult and sad times for every Russian. But why are you so worried? You still have time to get away..."

"I can't imagine what the servants are doing," said the countess, turning to her husband. "I've just been told nothing is ready. Someone has to take charge. One misses Mitenka at times like these. There'll be no end to it."
The count was about to say something but clearly restrained himself. He got up and moved toward the door.
At that moment Berg pulled out his handkerchief as if to blow his nose, and seeing the knot in it, paused and shook his head sadly and meaningfully.
"And I have a great favor to ask of you, Papa," he said.
"Hmm..." said the count, stopping.

"I was driving past Yusupov's house just now," Berg said with a laugh, "when the steward — a man I know — ran out and asked if I wanted to buy something. I went in out of curiosity, and there's a small chiffonier and a dressing table. You know how dear Vera wanted a chiffonier like that, and how we argued about it." (At the mention of the chiffonier and dressing table, Berg's tone involuntarily shifted to one of pleasure at his admirable domestic arrangements.) "And it's such a beauty! It has a pull-out drawer with a secret English compartment, you know! Vera has wanted one for ages. I'd love to surprise her. I noticed all those peasant carts in your yard. Could you let me have one? I'll pay the man well, and..."
The count frowned and coughed.
"Ask the countess. I don't give the orders."
"If it's inconvenient, please don't bother," said Berg. "I only wanted it so much, for dear Vera's sake."
"Oh, go to the devil, all of you! The devil, the devil, the devil!" cried the old count. "My head is spinning!"
And he left the room. The countess began to cry.
"Yes, Mama! Yes, these are very hard times!" said Berg.
Natasha left the room with her father and, as if struggling to reach some decision, first followed him, then ran downstairs.

Petya was on the porch, handing out weapons to the servants who were staying behind in Moscow. The loaded carts still stood in the yard. Two had been untied, and a wounded officer was climbing into one of them, helped by an orderly.
"Do you know what it's about?" Petya asked Natasha.
She understood he meant: what were their parents quarreling about? She didn't answer.
"It's because Papa wants to give up all the carts to the wounded," Petya said. "Vasilich told me. I think..."
"I think," Natasha nearly shouted, turning her furious face toward Petya, "I think it's so horrid, so vile, so... I don't know what! Are we miserable Germans?"
Her throat convulsed with sobs, and afraid of weakening and wasting the force of her anger, she turned and rushed headlong up the stairs.

Berg was sitting beside the countess, consoling her with the respectful attentiveness of a relative. The count stood pacing the room, pipe in hand, when Natasha burst in like a storm, her face distorted with rage, and rushed up to her mother.
"It's horrid! It's vile!" she screamed. "You can't possibly have ordered this!"
Berg and the countess stared at her, bewildered and frightened. The count stood still at the window, listening.
"Mama, it's impossible — look what's going on in the yard!" she cried. "They'll be left behind!"
"What's the matter with you? Who are 'they'? What do you want?"

"The wounded! It's impossible, Mama — it's monstrous! No, Mama darling, it's not right. Please forgive me, darling. Mama, what does it matter what we take? Just look at what's going on out there... Mama! It's impossible!"
The count stood by the window, listening, without turning around. Suddenly he sniffed and pressed his face closer to the glass.

The countess glanced at her daughter, saw the shame on Natasha's face — shame for her mother — saw her agitation, and understood why her husband wouldn't look at her now. She glanced around, completely flustered.
"Oh, do whatever you like! Am I stopping anyone?" she said, not giving in all at once.
"Mama, darling — forgive me!"
But the countess pushed her daughter away and went to her husband.
"My dear, you decide what's right. You know I don't understand these things," she said, dropping her eyes in shame.
"The eggs... the eggs are teaching the hen," the count muttered through tears of joy, and embraced his wife, who was glad to hide her embarrassed face against his chest.
"Papa! Mama! May I take charge? May I?" asked Natasha. "We'll still take all the most essential things."
The count nodded, and Natasha, moving at the same rapid pace she used when playing tag, ran through the ballroom to the anteroom and down to the yard.

The servants gathered around Natasha but couldn't believe the strange order she brought until the count himself, in his wife's name, confirmed it: give up all the carts to the wounded and put the trunks in the storerooms. When they understood, the servants set about this new task with pleasure and enthusiasm. It no longer seemed strange to them — on the contrary, it seemed the only thing to be done, just as a quarter of an hour earlier it had seemed perfectly natural to leave the wounded behind and load up the possessions.

The whole household, as if to make up for not having done it sooner, threw themselves eagerly into the new work of getting the wounded into the carts. The wounded dragged themselves out of their rooms and stood with pale but happy faces around the carts. Word spread to neighboring houses, and wounded men began arriving from down the street. Many asked not to have the carts unloaded but only to be allowed to sit on top of the luggage. But the unloading, once started, couldn't be stopped. It seemed not to matter whether half or all the belongings were left behind. Cases of china, bronzes, pictures, and mirrors that had been so carefully packed the night before now lay about the yard, and still they went on finding ways to unload more and fit in one more wounded man, and then another.
"We can take four more," said the steward. "They can have my trap — otherwise what will become of them?"
"Let them have my wardrobe cart," said the countess. "Dunyasha can ride with me in the carriage."

They unloaded the wardrobe cart and sent it to pick up wounded from a house two doors down. The whole household, servants included, was bright and animated. Natasha was in a state of joyful excitement she hadn't known for a long time.
"What can we strap this onto?" asked the servants, trying to fit a trunk onto the narrow footboard behind a carriage. "We have to keep at least one cart."
"What's in it?" asked Natasha.
"The count's books."
"Leave it. Vasilich will store it away. It's not needed."
The phaeton was packed with people, and there was some question about where Count Petya would sit.
"On the box. You'll sit on the box, won't you, Petya?" cried Natasha.

Sonya was busy all this time too, but her aim was quite different from Natasha's. She was putting away the things that had to be left behind and making a list of them, as the countess wished, and she tried to get as much taken along as possible.
